newsitem.title: USA: Muni firms should ask Congress for help on regs.
newsitem.headline: Muni firms should ask Congress for help on regs.

text.p: Bond firms that are fed up with the current web of U.S. regulation of the municipal market need to get organized and take their concerns to Capitol Hill, Ernest Patrikis, first vice president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York said on Saturday.
"I think part of the answer has to be legislative," said Patrikis, addressing the annual meeting of PSA The Bond Market Trade Association here.
"People have to take the time to say what is wrong and spell it out" to the U.S. Congress, said Patrikis, responding to a question from George Friedlander, a top analyst with Smith Barney Inc.

Friedlander had said that the muni market faces redundant and rigid written regulations by multiple agencies -- the Securities and Exchange Commission, the National Association of Securities Dealers, the Internal Revenue Service and the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board.

He said once a rule is put in place it is very hard to get regulators to fine-tune it, even if everyone agrees it needs revision. Freidlander added that he favors more oversight by examiners from SEC, IRS and NASD and less inflexible written regulations.

The muni market in the last three years has seen a raft of new rules out of Washington on issues like primary and secondary market disclosure, price transparency, political contributions to state and local government elected officials, escrow pricing or "yield burning," and others.

Patrikis said, "Regulatory agencies are what they are and do what they do. People have studied the beast. I don't want to get into all the big, wonderful, ugly aspects of the regulatory animal," he said.
"(But) it's incumbent on Congress to make sure we have a machine that works," Patrikis said. "We all need to educate legislators so that they understand that machine," Patrikis said.

Patrikis said less regulation may be the answer. "I think we can do more with less." The attitude in D.C. has shifted to an attitude that more supervision and less regulation may be the best tact, he said.
Patrikis, however, did not say which muni market standards should be revised, consolidated or revoked.
